title: The resolve that opens a puja
hookLine: before a puja, the priest names the age of the world and the family's name, then begins
carry: sankalpa: my small act, placed in God's time

lines: THE AGE OF THE WORLD, THEN TODAY'S DATE.
cards: Sunday morning at a grandmother's house, smelling of ghee and marigolds. A priest sits cross-legged before a small altar, and before a single flower is offered, he asks a question. Your name?

Then he takes a little water in his right hand and starts reciting, quickly, in Sanskrit: a long string about the second half of Brahma's life, the age of the White Boar, the Kali Yuga, this land, this day.
Only then does the puja begin.

teach.h: SANKALPA: THE RESOLVE THAT OPENS A PUJA.
teach.b: That recitation is the sankalpa, the resolve, and in a common form it begins with the whole of time. The second half of Brahma's life.

teach.h: OUR COSMIC DAY: THE WHITE BOAR.
teach.b: The kalpa, the cosmic day, called Shveta Varaha, the White Boar. That name carries a story.
The Bhagavata Purana tells that the earth once sank deep into the cosmic waters, and Brahma, just beginning to make the world, didn't know how to bring her back.
Then from his nostril came a tiny boar, no bigger than a thumb. It grew, and grew, until it filled the sky. It was Vishnu.

teach.h: VISHNU LIFTS THE EARTH ON HIS TUSKS.
teach.b: He dove into the flood, found the earth at the bottom, and lifted her up on his tusks while the sages sang his praise. Our cosmic day carries the name of that rescue.

teach.h: THE AGE, THE PLACE, THE DAY, THE PERSON, THE PURPOSE.
teach.b: Then it zooms in: this age, the Kali Yuga; this land; this year, month and day; this person, this family line; and this purpose. Here's the teaching: in Hindu worship, an offering isn't tossed off.

teach.h: MY SMALL ACT, PLACED IN GOD'S TIME.
teach.b: Before you act, you say who you are, where you stand in God's vast time, and why you're doing it. Then you offer it. A single flower becomes a deliberate act, set inside a story as old as the earth's rescue.
That's why the word turned up in the mantra days, and why yoga nidra borrowed it.

Swami Satyananda of the Bihar School, who set out the guided form, opens and closes the practice with a sankalpa: short, sincere, at the start and again near the end. Rest, like worship, begins on purpose.

how: Before a puja or a vrata, the priest or householder makes a sankalpa, often holding water in the right hand, naming the age of the world, the place, the date, the person and family line, and the purpose; guided yoga nidra opens and closes with a short sankalpa of the practitioner's own.

the sleep of yoga, opened and closed with a resolve

games.q: the priest asks your name and gotra before the puja even starts. why?
o: to keep a record for the temple office.
to make the sankalpa: who offers, when, where, and why.
to check you're allowed to attend.
games.why: the sankalpa places a small act on purpose inside God's time: the age, the place, the day, the person, the purpose.

practice: If you pray, cup a little water in your right hand, or simply cup the hand, and make a tiny sankalpa in your own words: who you are, today's date, where you are, and what you offer this rest for; then let the water go, or open the hand.
If you don't pray, say it as a quiet promise. Now lie back, hear the far sounds, the near ones, the breath, and rest. Near the end, say your sankalpa once more.

wordCard.voice: Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, which in its guided form opens and closes with a sankalpa, the same resolve that opens a puja.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sankalpa, resolve, intention. Made before a puja, and at the start and end of yoga nidra.

carryVoice: Your line: sankalpa, my small act, placed in God's time. The White Boar's day, and yours. Until tomorrow.
